The Frankfurt argument
1. Isabel is responsible for poisoning the coffee.
2. If Isabel is responsible for poisoning the coffee, then her act of poisoning the coffee is free.
3. Isabel’s act of poisoning the coffee is free. (1,2)
4. Isabel had no choice about the chip being inserted into her brain.
5. The chip being inserted into Isabel’s brain necessitates that she will poison the coffee. ————————————————————————-
C. An act can be free even if it is necessitated by facts about which the agent has no choice. (3,4,5)

It is natural to think that they must object to either (1) or (2), since (4) and (5) just specify features of the example. But (1) looks tough to deny.

The Frankfurt argument

How about (2)? One might agree that there is a tight link between freedom and responsibility without saying that every act for which you are responsible is a free act. Sometimes you can be responsible for acts which are not free but which are ‘downstream’ from free acts of yours.
